newsitem.title: SWEDEN: Sweden's Labour Board urges wait-and-see on EMU.
newsitem.headline: Sweden's Labour Board urges wait-and-see on EMU.

text.p: Sweden's Labour Market Board (AMS) said on Thursday that Sweden ought to wait before joining the European economic and monetary union (EMU) due to the current high levels of unemployment domestically.
"Unemployment is too high at current levels," AMS spokesman Mats Klingvall told Reuters.
"If it would rise without us being able to counteract it with every conceivable means it would be sad."
Klingvall was responding to an official government commission that investigated Swedish membership of EMU.
The commission, headed by Lars Calmfors, concluded Sweden should not join the EMU when it comes into force on January 1, 1999, but should instead wait to see how it develops.
Sweden's central bank, the Riksbank, last Friday rejected the commission's conclusions, saying Sweden will lose out unless it is among the first batch of countries to join.

"The economic benefits and the possibility of influencing the future direction of monetary policy leads the Riksbank's governing board to conclude that Sweden should participate in the EMU from the start," the Riksbank said in a statement.
But Klingvall said AMS did not agree with the Riksbank.
"Above all the possibility to have an independent monetary policy is of central importance," he said.
In the long run AMS was more neutral about EMU membership that the Calmfors commission.
"AMS thinks that Sweden should wait and do a new analysis," Klingvall said.
Meanwhile Pehr Wissen, the deputy managing director of one of Sweden's largest banks, Handelsbanken, said the commission lacked analysis of the disadvantages of a wait-and-see approach.
"Calmfors does not analyse the costs and inconvenience of entering the EMU late," Wissen said.
"I have worked with preparations ahead of EMU and to wait (with joining) is connected with costs and problems and this you must take into consideration when you make such a recommendation," he said.
Wissen said Sweden risked losing out if it waited.
"There is the risk that countries outside EMU will be discriminated against and not get full access to a common central bank," he said.
He also pointed to problems with needing double computer systems and the risk that some companies would leave Sweden.
"There is a simple philosophy for life that says that if you have decided to do something you should do it today and not wait," Wissen said.

The Swedish government is yet to make its final decision on Swedish membership of EMU but the ruling Social Democrats government was expected to detail its recommendation at the party congress in September this year.
